name: Marxist feminism
summary: Marxist feminism applies Marx's analysis of class and capital to women's oppression, arguing that it arose with private property and the monogamous family and is sustained by capitalism's reliance on women's unpaid domestic and reproductive labour. It holds that women's liberation requires bringing women into public production, socialising housework and childcare, and ending capitalism, rather than winning equality inside the existing order. Strands differ on whether to demand wages for housework or its socialisation, and on how far patriarchy is a separate system from capital.
notes: Strands differ on wages for housework (Dalla Costa, James, Federici) versus socialisation of care (Engels, Vogel). Only positions the sources state are answered; the other statements have no recorded position. Themes searched: family and marriage, housework and wages, class and revolution, race and class.
scope: Marxist feminism is the tradition that applies Marx's and Engels's analysis of class, property and the family to women's oppression, treating unpaid domestic and reproductive labour as part of how capitalism works and aiming at women's liberation through abolishing capitalism (Stanford Encyclopedia, Armstrong, Simply Psychology). The defining sources trace it from Engels's Origin of the Family and Zetkin through the 1960s-70s domestic labour debate (Benston, Dalla Costa and James, Federici, Vogel) and name its strands: wages for housework versus socialised care, and unitary versus dual-systems theory (Hartmann). Armstrong treats it together with socialist feminism and the Stanford entry lists dual-systems and socialist-feminist work beside it; the profile follows the Marxist strand where they differ. Liberal and radical feminisms are not its scope.
